claims.text: A branch is a name that points at a single commit. Creating one stores only the name and that commit's id; it copies no files and its cost does not grow with the size of the project.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entry 'branch'; git-branch documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'git branch <branchname> [<start-point>]'

claims.text: HEAD records which branch is checked out, except when it is detached and names a commit directly — a case this lesson only mentions. `git switch <branch>` moves HEAD to that branch and replaces the files in the working directory with the snapshot of the commit it points at.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entries 'HEAD' and 'detached HEAD'; git-switch documentation, DESCRIPTION

claims.text: Committing while standing on a branch writes a commit whose parent is the commit HEAD pointed at, then advances that one branch name to the new commit; no other branch name changes.
claims.source_hint: git-commit documentation, DESCRIPTION ('updates HEAD' / the current branch); gitglossary, entry 'branch'

claims.text: A remote is another repository recorded in your own under a short name; `git remote add <name> <path-or-url>` creates that record. `origin` is only the conventional name a clone gives the repository it came from.
claims.source_hint: git-remote documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'add'; gitglossary, entries 'remote' and 'origin'

claims.text: `origin/main` is a remote-tracking name maintained by your own repository as its record of where the remote's `main` stood at the last exchange; it is updated only by commands that contact the remote, and is not a branch you commit on.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entry 'remote-tracking branch'; git-fetch documentation, CONFIGURED REMOTE-TRACKING BRANCHES

claims.text: `git fetch` downloads commits and updates the remote-tracking names; on its own it integrates nothing into the branch you are standing on and leaves your files as they are — bringing the fetched commits in is the second step of `git pull`.
claims.source_hint: git-fetch documentation, DESCRIPTION; git-pull documentation, DESCRIPTION (fetch, then integrate)

claims.text: `git push` sends the commits of your branch to the remote repository and asks it to update its own branch to the commit yours points at.
claims.source_hint: git-push documentation, DESCRIPTION ('Updates remote refs using local refs')

claims.text: `git pull` runs `git fetch` and then integrates the fetched commits into the current branch; depending on how that second step is set up it changes local history and can stop part-way, after which `git status` reports the unfinished state instead of a clean branch line.
claims.source_hint: git-pull documentation, DESCRIPTION (fetch then merge/rebase); git-merge documentation, HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED; git-status documentation, output during an unfinished merge/rebase

claims.text: `git clone --bare <source> <dest>` creates a repository with no working directory — nowhere to check files out — which is how a repository meant only to be pushed to and fetched from is usually kept.
claims.source_hint: git-clone documentation, --bare

claims.text: A clone of a repository also brings across that repository's branches, so after `git fetch origin` this repository has `origin/feature/currency` and `origin/feature/shipping` as well as `origin/main`.
claims.source_hint: git-clone documentation, DESCRIPTION and --bare; git-fetch documentation, CONFIGURED REMOTE-TRACKING BRANCHES (the default refspec fetches all branches)

claims.text: `git branch --set-upstream-to=<remote-branch> <branch>` pairs a local branch with a remote-tracking name so that Git can report how far ahead or behind the branch is without contacting the remote.
claims.source_hint: git-branch documentation, -u/--set-upstream-to; git-status documentation, 'Short Format' tracking info

claims.text: `git branch -vv` prints one line per local branch: an asterisk marking the checked-out branch, the branch name, the abbreviated commit id, the upstream in square brackets when one is set, and the commit's subject line.
claims.source_hint: git-branch documentation, -v/-vv ('shows the upstream branch name as well')

claims.text: `git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all` draws the commits reachable from every reference, each marked with its own `*`, with the names pointing at a commit in round brackets after its id, and `|` columns plus `|/` lines drawing where the history splits.
claims.source_hint: git-log documentation, --graph, --decorate, --all; PRETTY FORMATS, oneline

claims.text: `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` prints the name of the branch currently checked out.
claims.source_hint: git-rev-parse documentation, --abbrev-ref

claims.text: Opinion: creating a feature branch is cheap and needs no deliberation, while bringing two branches back together is the step that needs care, because that is where the two lines of work have to be reconciled.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4 of foundation.l2.git-branches

claims.text: Git's own documentation calls the checked-out files the working tree; this lesson keeps the name working directory used by foundation.l2.git-mental-model.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entry 'working tree'

claims.text: `origin/HEAD` is a symbolic name in your repository whose target is the remote's default branch — the branch that remote starts on — which is why the captured graph prints it beside origin/main.
claims.source_hint: git-remote documentation, 'set-head' (the target of the symbolic ref refs/remotes/<name>/HEAD is the remote's default branch)

claims.text: The Git 2.46 manual page for `git switch` labels the command experimental and says its behaviour may change; `git checkout <branch>` performs the same move of HEAD and update of the working directory.
claims.source_hint: git-switch documentation, DESCRIPTION (the 'THIS COMMAND IS EXPERIMENTAL' notice); git-checkout documentation, DESCRIPTION ('git checkout <branch>')
